or_g_morning_glory_wall.blurb: Morning Glory Wall is one of the busiest faces at Smith Rock, a long welded-tuff wall of mostly bolted sport lines with a few trad and multipitch options mixed in. The grades climb from the high 5.8s through a thick block of 5.12 and 5.13, with a couple of 5.14 test pieces, so there is something for most levels, and the easiest lines draw the longest waits. The rock is clean and the bolts are solid. The wall takes full sun and gets hot by midday in summer, so many parties start early or come back for the evening.
or_g_morning_glory_wall.approach: Cross the footbridge, then follow the trails that contour along the hillside past the series of gullies; the wall runs between Cocaine Gully on one end and the Peanut on the other.

or_depot_the.blurb: The Depot is a band of tall basalt cliff beside the Deschutes River on the south edge of Bend, and it holds bouldering across a wide span of grades, from easy warm-ups to a handful of V8 and harder problems. Many of the boulders are around fifteen feet high, with decent landings, and the holds run ledgy and edgy with a good deal of crimping. The riverside setting keeps it cool and shaded for much of the day, and it sits on a popular walking trail, so expect hikers and dogs passing by. Chalk and cleaning keep most lines in good shape.
or_depot_the.approach: Follow the Deschutes River trail upstream from the south side of Bend. The cliff band opens up in a clearing beside the water, roughly a quarter to half hour on foot from the nearest parking.

or_u_red_wall.blurb: Red Wall is a reddish-purple face above the Misery Ridge Trail at Smith Rock, home to some of the park's better moderate multipitch routes along with a mix of sport and trad lines, a few steep crimpy pitches, and some low boulder problems at the base. Most climbs fall between 5.6 and 5.11, with the largest cluster around 5.9 to 5.11. The wall faces east, so it takes morning sun and goes into shade by early afternoon, which makes it a sensible choice on hot summer days. Loose rock can come down, so a helmet is worth wearing, especially while standing at the base.
or_u_red_wall.approach: Cross the bridge, then climb the early stretch of the Misery Ridge Trail until a marked spur leads up to the foot of the wall. It is a short, steady uphill walk.

or_3_catwalk_cliff.blurb: Catwalk Cliff stands on the west side of the Lower Gorge at Smith Rock, a wall of basalt columns where the climbing is mostly crack-oriented trad, with a handful of bolted lines. Grades center on 5.10 and 5.11 and run up to 5.12, with a few easier lines lower down. Columnar basalt rewards clean jamming and stemming, and the gorge setting down by the river is cooler than the main park walls, which makes it a popular retreat in warm weather. Getting here means a scrambly descent into the canyon, so allow extra time and take care on the way down.

or_2_wildfire_wall.blurb: Wildfire Wall sits on the west side of the Lower Gorge at Smith Rock, on basalt columns that favor crack climbing. Most of the routes are trad, with a smaller group of bolted sport lines, and nearly all of them fall between 5.10 and 5.12. Finger and hand cracks, thin stemming and the occasional bulge make for sustained, technical pitches, and the setting beside the river is a cooler alternative to the sun-baked walls up top. The walk in follows past the small Parched Cat cliff, and the descent into the canyon involves some scrambling.

or_skinner_butte_aka_the_columns.blurb: The Columns are a small urban crag in downtown Eugene, a wall of basalt columns left behind by old quarrying. Nearly everything is trad or top rope, short lines of roughly fifty feet with plenty of cracks, so it suits both crack practice and learning to place gear. Most grades sit between 5.6 and 5.12, and the ratings can feel inconsistent. The face looks west and picks up sun from afternoon into evening, so mornings are cooler in summer. The car-to-rock walk is under a minute, and it gets crowded with after-work climbers. The rock is mostly solid but pieces do break loose now and then.

or_french_s_dome.blurb: French's Dome is a lone andesite dome in the forest on the west side of Mount Hood, with bolted routes of roughly 80 to 160 feet. The climbing is sporty, crimpy and pumpy, with grades spread from easy 5th class to the low 5.13s, though most of the lines are 5.11 and 5.12. Anchors are chains, and most of the routes are on the left half of the dome as you arrive. The dome is shaded for much of the day, so afternoons are the best bet, and snow makes it a late-spring-to-early-fall crag. Quiet and secluded, with old-growth forest around it.

or_jungle_cliff.blurb: Jungle Cliff is one of the smaller walls at Broughton Bluff, the basalt crag on the edge of Portland at the mouth of the Columbia Gorge. It is known for its columns and holds almost entirely sport climbs, with a core of 5.11 and 5.12 and a good number of 5.13s, so it leans toward intermediate and strong sport climbers. The newer routes can be dirty and dusty until they see more traffic. The bluff stays damp through the cool season, and late spring through fall is the better window. Poison oak grows near the trails.
